authority: AMS (Arbeitsmarktservice) + Magistrat Wien MA 35 (Vienna) / Bezirkshauptmannschaft (other Länder)
form_name: Antrag auf Erteilung eines Aufenthaltstitels — Rot-Weiss-Rot-Karte
deadline_label: Apply from country of habitual residence; minimum 60 days before intended start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: One Rot-Weiss-Rot-Karte covers all categories. Applications for the initial card are lodged at the Austrian diplomatic representation in the applicant's country of habitual residence.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Four distinct subtypes exist — Besonders Hochqualifizierte (points system), Fachkräfte in Mangelberufen (AMS shortage list), Sonstige Schlüsselkräfte (employer-specific salary floor), and Absolventen (Austrian university graduates) — each with different points thresholds, salary floors, and AMS labour-market check requirements. Applying under the wrong subtype is the leading cause of rejection. The AMS Mangelberufsliste is updated quarterly; a profession may no longer qualify by the time the application is assembled.
non_obvious_action_required: Have the employer confirm which RWR subtype applies before gathering documents. Verify the employee's occupation currently appears on the AMS Mangelberufsliste if using the Fachkraft route — check the live list, not a cached copy. Engage an Austrian immigration lawyer to confirm subtype and assemble the points dossier.
source: Bundesministerium für Inneres — migration.gv.at, Rot-Weiss-Rot-Karte overview

form_name: Antrag auf Erteilung eines Aufenthaltstitels — EU-Blaue Karte
deadline_label: Apply from country of habitual residence; minimum 60 days before start; requires confirmed job offer with salary above indexed threshold
non_obvious_official_guidance: The EU Blue Card requires a recognised higher education qualification and a job offer with a gross annual salary of at least 1.5 times the Austrian average gross annual salary.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The salary threshold is indexed annually; for 2024–25 it stands at approximately €66,000 gross per year for most professions and ~€55,000 for designated shortage professions (STEM, ICT, healthcare). Only contractually guaranteed base salary counts — bonus, allowances, and equity do not. Internal HR teams frequently calculate the threshold against monthly net pay rather than annual gross, causing the application to be filed with insufficient documentation or for an ineligible candidate.
non_obvious_action_required: Pull the guaranteed annual gross base salary from the employment contract and verify it clears the current-year indexed threshold before starting the application. Check the live threshold at migration.gv.at each year — it changes. Exclude any variable component and have the employer confirm the contractual figure in writing.
source: Bundesministerium für Inneres — migration.gv.at, EU Blue Card Austria

authority: Austrian Embassy or Consulate in country of habitual residence
deadline_label: Apply after RWR/Blue Card approval letter issued; allow 2–4 weeks for consulate processing; book appointment immediately on receipt of approval
non_obvious_official_guidance: Nationals of certain third countries require a national D-Visa to enter Austria for the purpose of taking up employment. The D-Visa is issued on the basis of an already-approved residence title.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Citizens of the US, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, and a handful of other nationalities are visa-exempt for Schengen stays up to 90 days and may enter Austria and collect their RWR Card after arrival without a prior D-Visa. Citizens of most other non-EU countries do require the D-Visa and cannot convert status in Austria — if they enter on a visa-exempt short stay without first obtaining the D-Visa, they must leave Austria to collect the physical card, disrupting the start date. Confusing Schengen visa exemption with work-entry rights is common and costly.
non_obvious_action_required: Check the employee's nationality against the current Austrian visa-exemption list before booking travel. If a D-Visa is required, book the Austrian consular appointment the same day the RWR approval letter arrives — backlogs at some missions run 4–6 weeks. Confirm whether the relevant consulate accepts online appointment booking or requires a phone queue before starting.
source: Austrian Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs (BMEIA) — Visa requirements for Austria

deadline_label: Confirmed address with Unterkunftgeber signature capability needed before Day 1–3 Meldezettel deadline
non_obvious_official_guidance: A permanent registered address (Hauptwohnsitz) is required to complete Meldezettel registration, collect a residence permit, open a bank account, and register with the Finanzamt.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Vienna's private rental market requires up to 3 months' gross rent as Kaution plus first month upfront; landlords routinely demand an Austrian bank reference or local income proof — neither of which a newly arriving employee has. Maklergebühr (agent commission) is legally chargeable to the tenant at up to 2 months' rent plus 20% VAT. Critically, the Meldezettel form requires the Unterkunftgeber's (accommodation provider's) countersignature — if the landlord is unreachable, the 3-day registration deadline triggers a cascade failure: no Meldezettel means no bank account, no permit collection, and no Finanzamt registration.
non_obvious_action_required: Arrange employer-sponsored temporary accommodation or a serviced apartment (Aparthotel) before departure — these operators guarantee same-day Meldezettel countersigning as standard. Warn the employee that private rentals on willhaben.at or immobilienscout24.at require Austrian income proof; the employer may need to provide a Bürgschaft (guarantee letter) for the first contract.
source: Österreichisches Mietrechtsgesetz (MRG); WKO Austria — Mietrecht für Mieter

authority: Meldeamt (Magistrat / Gemeindeamt in municipality of residence)
deadline_label: Within 3 days of moving in — legally enforceable; fines up to €726 for late registration
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under the Meldegesetz, all persons residing in Austria must register their address at the local Meldeamt within three days of moving in. Both the resident and the accommodation provider (Unterkunftgeber) must sign the Meldezettel.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The 3-day deadline is strictly enforced and spot-check fines are issued. The Hauptwohnsitz (primary residence) designation — not Nebenwohnsitz (secondary residence) — is required for bank account opening, permit collection, Steuernummer assignment, and all official correspondence; registering as Nebenwohnsitz to preserve a notional home-country address is a widespread mistake that blocks every subsequent bureaucratic step. Hotel and serviced-apartment operators routinely countersign the form on the same day; private landlords sometimes create delays by requiring in-person Meldeamt attendance.
non_obvious_action_required: Register Hauptwohnsitz on Day 1 or Day 2 — never wait for day 3. Download the Meldezettel PDF from oesterreich.gv.at before arrival and have it pre-completed. In Vienna, registrations can be completed at any Magistratisches Bezirksamt without an appointment. Confirm the accommodation provider will countersign before booking the stay.

deadline_label: Mandatory after 3 months of continuous residence; best obtained in arrival week to unblock bank, Finanzamt, and employer HR systems
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU, EEA, and Swiss nationals exercising free movement rights in Austria for more than 3 months must obtain an Anmeldebescheinigung from the competent authority, as required by the NAG (Niederlassungs- und Aufenthaltsgesetz § 9).
non_obvious_actual_reality: Most EU/EEA employees skip this step believing their EU passport grants automatic unrestricted residence without registration. Austrian banks, the Finanzamt, and many employer HR departments treat the Anmeldebescheinigung as proof of legal long-term residence and will not proceed without it. Queues at Vienna MA 35 routinely run 2–3 hours on walk-in days. Norwegian, Icelandic, and Liechtenstein (EEA non-EU) nationals are fully eligible but are frequently unaware they are included. Swiss nationals have an equivalent obligation under the CH–EU Agreement on Free Movement of Persons.
non_obvious_action_required: Apply within the first week — not when the 3-month statutory clock expires. Bring: valid passport or national ID, Meldezettel showing Hauptwohnsitz, employment contract, and a recent employer confirmation letter. No appointment is required at Vienna MA 35 but arrive before opening to manage the queue.
source: NAG (Niederlassungs- und Aufenthaltsgesetz) § 9; migration.gv.at — Citizens of the EU/EEA

field_label: Collect RWR Card / EU Blue Card Biometric Residence Permit
deadline_label: Collect within 4 weeks of arrival; in-person biometric fingerprint appointment required
non_obvious_official_guidance: Once the residence title is approved, the applicant is notified to attend an in-person biometric data collection appointment (Personalisierungsabnahme) and subsequently collect the physical chip card at the issuing authority.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Vienna MA 35 biometric appointment backlogs routinely run 6–10 weeks, meaning the employee may be legally working in Austria for months before holding the physical card. The interim Aufenthaltsbestätigung (approval confirmation letter) is valid for right-to-work verification but is not accepted by all HR compliance systems or bank identity checks. HR teams that require the physical card number before onboarding completion will face a stalled process.
non_obvious_action_required: Book the biometric appointment at MA 35 immediately on arrival — do not wait for the formal notification letter. HR should retain a certified copy of the card upon collection and calendar the expiry date (typically 24 months for the initial RWR Card). Set a renewal alert at the 21-month mark; do not wait for the card to expire.
source: Magistrat Wien MA 35 — Aufenthaltstitel: biometrische Daten und Abholung

authority: Österreichische Gesundheitskasse (ÖGK) via employer ELDA registration
form_name: ELDA pre-registration (employer-filed); e-card issued and posted automatically
deadline_label: Employer must file ELDA registration before or on Day 1 of employment; physical e-card arrives by post within 4–6 weeks
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employers are legally required to register employees with the Österreichische Gesundheitskasse via the ELDA (Elektronischer Datenaustausch) system before commencement of employment. Mandatory coverage (health, accident, pension, unemployment) begins from Day 1.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The physical e-card takes 4–6 weeks to arrive by post; in the interim the Sozialversicherungsauszug (insurance record extract) downloaded from meineSV.at serves as proof of coverage for prescriptions, doctor visits, and hospital admissions. The Sozialversicherungsnummer (SVNR, 10 digits) assigned at registration is distinct from the Steuernummer — both are needed for different official purposes and confusing them causes processing delays throughout year one. The SVNR is a lifelong identifier that stays with the individual even after leaving Austria.
non_obvious_action_required: Confirm with payroll that the ELDA pre-registration was filed before Day 1. Register on meineSV.at immediately to download the Sozialversicherungsauszug as interim proof of coverage. Issue the employee their SVNR in writing on Day 1 — they need it at every medical appointment before the physical e-card arrives.

authority: Austrian commercial banks (Erste Bank, Raiffeisen, BAWAG, Bank Austria) or EU-licensed fintechs (N26, Revolut AT)
deadline_label: Before first payroll run; employer payroll systems typically require an AT IBAN within 2–3 weeks of start
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under EU payment services law (transposed via ZaDiG 2018), all legal residents in Austria are entitled to open a basic Basiskonto regardless of nationality or employment status.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Traditional Austrian banks routinely require a Meldezettel showing Hauptwohnsitz, passport, employment contract, and the physical RWR Card or Anmeldebescheinigung before opening a current account — newly arriving employees often lack one or more of these in their first weeks. EU-licensed fintechs (N26 Germany GmbH, Revolut) operating in Austria under EU passporting can open an account via passport and video selfie with no Meldezettel or permit required, providing a reliable bridging AT IBAN. Salary is paid via SEPA credit transfer; foreign IBANs are technically valid under SEPA but are frequently rejected by Austrian payroll systems in practice.
non_obvious_action_required: Open an N26 or Revolut AT account on or before arrival day using passport only, to guarantee a working AT IBAN exists for Day 1 payroll. Open a traditional Austrian bank account once Meldezettel and RWR Card or Anmeldebescheinigung are in hand. Alert payroll to hold the first salary run until a confirmed AT IBAN is on file.
source: ZaDiG 2018 (Zahlungsdienstegesetz) implementing EU PSD2; WKO Austria — Das Zahlungskonto

field_label: Austrian Tax Number (Steuernummer) and FinanzOnline Registration
deadline_label: Within first month; required before filing Arbeitnehmerveranlagung or claiming any tax relief
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employees subject to Lohnsteuer (wage tax) do not need to separately register with the Finanzamt — the employer withholds and remits Lohnsteuer automatically. A Steuernummer is assigned by the competent Finanzamt upon first contact.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Steuernummer is distinct from the Sozialversicherungsnummer (SVNR) and the two are routinely confused in official correspondence, causing processing delays. Austria taxes worldwide income of tax residents — an employee who also has rental income, investment income, or who worked in another country in the same calendar year may be required to file a full Einkommensteuererklärung rather than the optional Arbeitnehmerveranlagung, and penalties apply for underpayment. Double taxation treaty (Doppelbesteuerungsabkommen, DBA) relief on foreign-source income must be actively claimed; it is not applied automatically by the employer.
non_obvious_action_required: Register on FinanzOnline (finanzonline.bmf.gv.at) within the first month to obtain the Steuernummer and activate the online tax account. If the employee had any income in another country during the same calendar year, flag this to a Steuerberater immediately — the residency-start-date proration and foreign tax credits must be claimed proactively.
source: EStG (Einkommensteuergesetz) §§ 1–2; Bundesministerium für Finanzen (BMF) — Einkommensteuer / Lohnsteuer

form_name: Erklärung zur Arbeitnehmerveranlagung (L1 form, filed online via FinanzOnline)
deadline_label: Voluntary filing by 30 April of the following year via FinanzOnline; 5-year retroactive claim window applies
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employees may voluntarily file an Arbeitnehmerveranlagung to claim deductions against Lohnsteuer already withheld. If no return is filed, the Finanzamt may issue an automatic simplified assessment (automatische Arbeitnehmerveranlagung).
non_obvious_actual_reality: Most Austrian employees receive a refund averaging €400–900 on voluntary filing because Lohnsteuer is deducted on gross income without accounting for expenses. International employees routinely miss: Homeoffice-Pauschale (home-office flat rate up to €300/year), Pendlerpauschale (commuting allowance), professional membership fees, work-related education, and relocation costs. The 5-year retroactive claim window is widely unknown — employees who never filed in earlier years can reclaim Lohnsteuer overpayments for years 1–4 retrospectively. If any non-Austrian income, multiple Austrian employers, or a multi-country year arises, mandatory filing replaces the voluntary option.
non_obvious_action_required: File via FinanzOnline by 30 April each year for priority processing. Retain all professional expense receipts throughout the year. If any non-Austrian income or multi-country employment situation arises, engage a Steuerberater — automatic assessments will not handle these correctly and late-payment interest applies.
source: EStG § 41 (Arbeitnehmerveranlagung); BMF — employee tax assessment guidance

form_name: Antrag auf Erteilung Rot-Weiss-Rot-Karte Plus / Verlängerungsantrag RWR-Karte
field_label: RWR Card Plus Upgrade or Two-Year Card Renewal
deadline_label: RWR Card Plus available after 12 months of employment with initial card; renewal due 90 days before 2-year card expiry
non_obvious_official_guidance: The Rot-Weiss-Rot-Karte Plus is issued to holders of an initial RWR Card who have been employed for at least 12 months and whose employment relationship is continuing. It grants unrestricted access to the entire Austrian labour market for 3 years.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Most employees and HR teams are unaware that the 12-month Plus upgrade is available significantly earlier than the 2-year card renewal cycle — missing it keeps the employee employer-locked for an unnecessary extra 12 months. The RWR Card Plus also permits changing employer or taking a second job without a new AMS labour-market check — a major practical freedom not communicated in standard employer onboarding. Vienna MA 35 processing for Plus applications runs 8–12 weeks; late filing risks a status gap.
non_obvious_action_required: Calendar a 10-month check-in with the employee: confirm employment continues and file the RWR Card Plus application before the 12-month anniversary. Set a separate 21-month alert for the 2-year full renewal if the Plus upgrade is not pursued. Build both milestones into the HR mobility tracking system on Day 1.

authority: Magistrat Wien MA 35 (Vienna) / Bezirkshauptmannschaft / BFA (Bundesamt für Fremdenwesen und Asyl)
field_label: EU Long-Term Residence Permit (Daueraufenthalt-EU) — Eligible After 5 Years
deadline_label: Eligible after 5 years of continuous legal residence; apply 3 months before the 5-year anniversary
non_obvious_official_guidance: The Daueraufenthalt-EU requires 5 years of uninterrupted legal residence in Austria, stable and sufficient income, comprehensive health insurance, and B1 German language skills plus civic knowledge (Module 2 of the Österreichischer Integrationsfonds Integrationsprüfung or equivalent).
non_obvious_actual_reality: The 5-year continuity clock is broken by any single absence exceeding 6 consecutive months or cumulative absences exceeding 10 months in the qualifying period — frequent business travellers may unknowingly disqualify themselves. The B1 Integrationsprüfung (Module 2) is administered by the ÖIF; course booking lead times run 3–4 months and exams can only be sat at approved Austrian centres. An employee who waits until year 5 to book the language course will miss the application window. The exam is the most commonly overlooked administrative blocker for otherwise-eligible long-term employees.
non_obvious_action_required: Track all absences from Austria from Day 1 using a travel log — retroactive reconstruction at year 4 is unreliable. Book the ÖIF B1 Integrationsprüfung course at the year-4 mark to allow time for re-sits. Engage an immigration advisor at year 4 to audit the full continuity record, income documentation, and application package.

authority: Pensionsversicherungsanstalt (PVA) / Österreichische Gesundheitskasse (ÖGK) / home-country social security authority (posted workers)
form_name: Versicherungsdatenauszug via meineSV.at / A1 Portable Document (EU posted workers)
field_label: ASVG Social Insurance Record and A1 Portability Certificate
deadline_label: Annual record review; A1 certificate must be obtained before assignment begins for any EU-posted worker
non_obvious_official_guidance: All employees working in Austria are mandatorily covered under the ASVG for health, accident, pension, and unemployment insurance. Employees temporarily posted to Austria from another EU/EEA member state may remain in their home social security system if a valid A1 certificate is held.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Austria's combined social insurance contribution rate is approximately 39.8% of gross salary (21.2% employer / 18.6% employee in 2024), among the highest in the EU. Employees temporarily posted to Austria from another EU country without a valid A1 certificate face mandatory ASVG contributions in addition to home-country contributions — de facto double payment that is extremely difficult to recover retroactively. EU-country prior pension periods can be totalized toward Austrian pension entitlement under EU Regulation 883/2004, but totalization must be actively claimed by the employee; it is never applied automatically. Short-assignment employees routinely miss the A1 requirement entirely and face retroactive ASVG demands after audit.
non_obvious_action_required: Retrieve the Versicherungsdatenauszug from meineSV.at annually to verify all insured periods are correctly recorded. For employees posted to Austria from another EU country, ensure the home-country authority issues the A1 certificate before the assignment start date — not after. For employees with multi-country career histories, engage a Steuerberater or social security specialist to assess totalization rights before departure from Austria.
source: ASVG; EU Regulation 883/2004 (coordination of social security); meineSV.at — Versicherungsdatenauszug
